hints.content:
Based on the second part of the fundamental theorem of calculus, $g$ is an antiderivative of $f$:

$g'=f$

This table summarizes the relationship between various properties of a function $f$ and its antiderivative $g$:

When the function $f$ is... | The antiderivative $g=\displaystyle\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ is...
:-: | :-:
Positive $+$ | Increasing $\nearrow$
Negative $-$ | Decreasing $\searrow$
Increasing $\nearrow$ | Concave up $\cup$
Decreasing $\searrow$ | Concave down $\cap$
Changes sign / crosses the $x$-axis | Extremum point
Extremum point | Inflection point

This is an appropriate calculus-based justification for the fact that $g$ has an inflection point at $x=c$:

$f$ has a relative minimum at $x=c$.

The curve starts on the positive y-axis, moves downward to a relative minimum at (c, 0), moves upward to a relative maximum in quadrant 1, moves downward and ends in quadrant 4.](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/d933bf41fefc20fdcf5e3e1fe4a104549a3e5107)

Let $g(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$.

**What is an appropriate calculus-based justification for the fact that $g$ has an inflection point at $x=c$?**

[[☃ radio 1]]

choices.clue: When a function has an inflection point, its *second* derivative must be equal to $0$. However, $f$ is the first derivative of $g$.
The concavity of $f$ doesn't affect the concavity of $g$. $f$ could be concave down and still $g$ could have an inflection point. Try to think about the relationship between $f$ and $g$.
